nameStory: The name 'honeysuckle' comes from the old English tradition of children sucking the sweet nectar from the tubular flowers — nature's candy! It's also called 'woodbine' because of its vigorous twining habit, literally binding itself around trees and shrubs as it climbs toward the light.
description: Common honeysuckle is a vigorous climbing vine that can reach 15-20 feet tall, wrapping itself around trees, fences, and anything else it can grasp. This European native produces clusters of incredibly fragrant, tubular flowers that are cream-colored when they open and age to golden yellow. The oval leaves grow in pairs along the stems, and the whole plant has a somewhat woody base despite being a vine. While beautiful and sweetly scented, it can be quite aggressive in spreading.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tubular flowers about 2 inches long appear in terminal clusters, starting cream-white and aging to deep golden yellow. The fragrance is intensely sweet and can be detected from several feet away, especially in evening when it's strongest.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves grow in opposite pairs along the stem and feel smooth to the touch. The uppermost pairs just below the flower clusters are fused together, forming a cup-like disk that the stem appears to grow through.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A vigorous twining vine that spirals clockwise as it climbs, with stems that become woody at the base. New growth feels slightly sticky and has a pleasant, mild fragrance when crushed.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small red berries appear in clusters where the flowers were, ripening in late summer. The berries have a slightly waxy feel and are considered mildly toxic to humans.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature stems develop thin, papery bark that peels in narrow strips, revealing lighter colored wood underneath. Young stems are smooth and green to reddish-brown.

habitat: Common honeysuckle thrives in woodland edges, old gardens, and disturbed areas with partial to full sun. It prefers well-drained soils but is quite adaptable, often found climbing over stone walls, fences, and native shrubs. Look for it in areas where European plants were historically cultivated, as it readily escapes garden settings.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge early and flowers begin blooming in late spring, filling the air with their distinctive sweet perfume that's strongest in the evening.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs in early summer with the most intense fragrance, followed by small red berries forming in late summer as flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may show some yellowing before dropping, and red berries ripen and persist, making them visible against the bare stems.
seasonality.winter: Leafless vines show their twining growth pattern clearly, with papery peeling bark and sometimes persistent dried flower heads at branch tips.

funFact: Common honeysuckle flowers actually change their scent throughout the day — they're most fragrant in the evening to attract night-flying moths for pollination, but by morning the scent has faded significantly as the flowers shift their strategy to attract different pollinators!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Japanese honeysuckle, but common honeysuckle has the distinctive fused upper leaves that form cups around the stem, while Japanese honeysuckle's leaves never fuse. Remember: 'Common has cups, Japanese just has regular leaf pairs.'
contextualKnowledge: While called 'common' honeysuckle, it's actually quite rare in New England with only 5 recorded observations, likely because it's not as aggressive here as the infamous Japanese honeysuckle. Many people assume any climbing honeysuckle is Japanese, but this European species was actually grown in colonial gardens long before Japanese honeysuckle arrived.
compareHints: Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers. American fly-honeysuckle is a completely different growth form — an upright shrub rather than a vine — and produces paired blue berries instead of red clusters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
